Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2611.03627v1 [cs.LG] 02 Nov 2026 Not All Reasoning Generalizes: A Case Study on Learning Generalizable Reasoning Strategies in RLVR Ziqi Pang Yu-Xiong Wang Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Email: {ziqip2,yxw}@illinois.edu Abstract Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can enable generalizable improvement for large language model (LLM) reasoning. This paper studies how to incentivize such generalization via reasoning strategies . We study this question with a controllable equation-solving framework: finding multiple inputs x x for equations f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y , where f f is a non-bijective string function. This setting makes reasoning strategies observable while supporting a clear definition of easy-to-hard out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts, e.g. , more solutions, longer y y , etc. We uncover a subtle RLVR failure: it teaches the model to solve in-distribution tasks with high accuracy and structured step-by-step derivation, yet under OOD shifts, the same model abandons derivation and collapses to ineffective brute-force enumeration, causing sharp accuracy drops. This observation reveals the deeper challenges of RLVR generalization as it is neither incapable base model nor reward hacking , since the model succeeds in-distribution with the correct reasoning strategy. The key to mitigating this failure is an indirect intervention that surprisingly helps: co-training with bijective inversion tasks. Although these bijective tasks are actually not uniformly harder and even further from the non-bijective OOD evaluation, they make derivation more certain and substantially restore the correct strategy and accuracy under OOD shifts. This effect further motivates our theoretical analysis: outcome-only RLVR can shape reasoning processes through implicitly crediting the effective reasoning strategies more, even without process supervision. To conclude, our analysis framework and findings systematically reveal the crucial role and incentivization of reasoning strategies in RLVR generalization under OOD shifts. Code is available at https://github.com/ziqipang/rl_meta_thinking . 1 Introduction Applying reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) to large language models (LLMs) has shown surprising generalization capabilities. Rather than imitating fixed traces, RLVR incentivizes meta-level reasoning strategies that can transfer to out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks. For instance, Yuan et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2026a) show that general reasoning strategies like composing and case analysis are shown to be transferable from the training tasks to novel domains ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . Such positive cases, however, cannot establish transfer as a general rule. We ask the complementary question: when and why does RLVR generalization fail? However, we realize that such generalization of reasoning strategies has not been thoroughly investigated. Previous studies mostly understand RLVR generalization from its relationship with the base models ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) without clearly categorizing individual reasoning strategies and analyzing their OOD generalization. To this end, we start by building a controllable framework that clearly defines OOD generalization and categorizes reasoning strategies. As in Fig. 1 a , we construct a set of string functions f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) inspired by Yuan et al. (2026) , and let the LLM address this inverse problem: recovering multiple inputs x x such that f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y ( y y is a provided string output). This task mirrors solving math equations and tracing bugs in coding. More importantly, we construct the functions f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) f(\cdot) to be non-bijective and require LLMs to output k > 1 k>1 different solutions. This framework thus clearly splits in-distribution and OOD tasks, where the OOD tasks are built from held-out functions and made harder via longer strings y y and more required solutions k k . On this controllable framework, we observe that RLVR can reliably teach an LLM to perform reasoning effectively in-distribution , showing reliable derivation strategies step-by-step and enumerating characters only when needed, as Fig. 1 b . However, this model, named Mono , shows drastically different behaviors on harder OOD tasks: it abandons the strategy of derivation, and instead, relies on ineffective brute-force enumeration of all the digits simultaneously (Fig. 1 c ). Such an observation marks an important revelation: an LLM can learn to perform effective reasoning strategies in-distribution , yet drastically falls back to worse strategies in OOD scenarios . Such an observation is nuanced as it is not related to the commonly known RLVR failures like incapable base models or reward hacking, as the model is following valid reasoning traces to achieve high accuracy during training. Therefore, we are studying real generalization challenges under this setting. Figure 1: (a) To clearly define OOD generalization for LLM reasoning, we construct a controllable framework via solving string function equations, mirroring real-world math and coding. (b) We categorize two major reasoning strategies, the more effective Derivation and or total brute-force Enumeration . (c) We reveal how reasoning strategies reflect the challenges of OOD generalization. The Mono model learns derivation for ID cases, yet drastically collapses to enumeration for OOD. With Mixed better incentivizing the derivation strategy, it achieves much better OOD accuracy under similar ID performance. These form a systematic framework of understanding RLVR generalization. This diagnosis suggests that the key is not merely to improve training accuracy but to change which reasoning strategies RLVR incentivizes. We therefore introduce a seemingly indirect intervention for the task: co-training with bijective tasks that only asks for one solution x x for f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y . The intuition is to decrease the search space in non-bijective functions and encourage step-by-step derivation with larger certainties. Importantly, this intervention is surprising because the bijective tasks are not uniformly harder and are even further away from the non-bijective OOD evaluation requiring multiple solutions. Nevertheless, the Mixed model with this intervention successfully restores the behavior of utilizing the derivation strategy and leads to significantly better OOD accuracy (Fig. 1 c ). Such effectiveness inspires us to understand how better reasoning strategies can be incentivized from RLVR. As in Fig. 1 b , we view the reasoning process as progressively shrinking the candidate solution space. This analogy clearly distinguishes the derivation and enumeration: derivation is more effective by structurally pruning multiple candidates in a single step, while enumeration can only contribute marginally by eliminating one wrong candidate. Therefore, the reasoning strategies like derivation can contribute more bits per step, and can more easily generalize to harder scenarios, i.e. , those requiring more bits. By connecting this with RL algorithms theoretically, we show that even outcome-only RLVR can implicitly credit such effective reasoning processes without process supervision, explaining how reasoning strategies could emerge from RLVR. Beyond theory, our probing of the hidden states and reasoning trace audit also qualitatively shows how reasoning strategies could be a principled way to understand the generalization behaviors of LLMs in RLVR. Our study presents a systematic analysis of RLVR generalization via reasoning strategies: (i) A controlled counter-example of RLVR teaching correct in-distribution reasoning strategies that nevertheless change and fail under OOD shifts : a subtle failure distinct from incapable base models. (ii) A principled intervention on reasoning strategies significantly enhances OOD generalization, which reveals the pivotal role of reasoning strategies in the transferable improvements of RLVR. (iii) The theoretical analysis explaining how more effective and generalizable reasoning strategies can be incentivized naturally via RLVR from a information per reasoning step perspective. (iv) Reasoning trace inspection and probing of the model’s hidden states qualitatively reveal how reasoning strategies are principled aspects to understand RLVR generalization. Considering the importance of RLVR generalization, we hope this framework has provided a comprehensive yet nuanced understanding of LLM reasoning and generalization through synthetic and controllable data, with the same spirit as prior work that has inspired us ( Allen-Zhu & Li, 2025a ; Ye et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Yin et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . 2 Related Work RLVR Generalization. RLVR has produced a growing set of positive generalization results: such as general reasoning and agentic capabilities enhancement after math/coding-oriented RL ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Kimi Team et al., 2025 ) , carefully structured RL expands benchmark coverage ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) , synthetic strings showing compositional expansion ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , and game/puzzles improve to reasoning benchmarks ( Liu et al., 2026a ; Zhao et al., 2025a ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Tong et al., 2026 ) . Meanwhile, some studies argue that RLVR gains can also be re-distribution of the base model behaviors or spurious observations ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2025b ; Gandhi et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026b ; Wu et al., 2026a ) . Our work, however, is complementary to both sides of this debate. Instead, we show a strategy-level and nuanced inspection of how RLVR impacts the reasoning strategies of LLMs and the information effectiveness for a strategy to generalize to harder OOD domains. Specifically, a most crucial discovery is that RLVR can teach a model to solve the in-distribution task with the intended reasoning strategy, yet that strategy can collapse into a brittle alternative on OOD domains, which is different from either incapable-base-model failures or reward-hacking artifacts. RLVR Algorithms. Representative LLM post-training algorithms include PPO-style RLHF ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , preference optimization like DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , and outcome-based methods like GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . With the effectiveness of GRPO for math and coding, recent work has extended it through DAPO, Dr. GRPO, GSPO, and other variants or recipes that address MoE stability, length or token-level bias, sampling efficiency, etc ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Wen et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) . We mainly use the basic DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , as our focus is the underlying meta-level reasoning behavior and generalization. Investigating LLMs via Controllable and Synthetic Data. Synthetic data is a crucial tool to analyze the LLM behaviors reliably, especially represented by the physics of LLMs ( Allen-Zhu & Li, 2025a ; Ye et al., 2025a ; Ye et al., 2025b ; Allen-Zhu & Li, 2024 ; Allen-Zhu & Li, 2025b ; Allen-Zhu & Li, 2025c ) . In LLM reasoning, synthetic data has become essential for understanding generalization, since they provide clear boundaries: symbolic or length-controlled math variants ( Mirzadeh et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) , synthesized arithmetic probes ( Ye et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Yin et al., 2025 ) , and controlled agentic dynamics ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . In addition, some studies also use causal interventions, circuit analyses, and probing to identify internal algorithms or encoded information ( Olsson et al., 2022 ; Meng et al., 2022 ; Voita & Titov, 2020 ; Gurnee & Tegmark, 2024 ) . The work that inspires this work most is Yuan et al. (2026) , which understands how meta-level reasoning skills like composing could be generalized in RL. We adopt this controlled-data philosophy but use it for a different purpose: rather than using synthetic tasks only to avoid contamination or measure extrapolation, our inversion framework makes the model’s reasoning strategy observable and can reveal the nuances of RLVR generalization. With our synthetic framework, we uncover the collapse of RLVR in OOD scenarios, demonstrate principled interventions, and propose theoretical analysis. 3 Research Framework 3.1 Task Format and Principles Principles. Our investigation centers on which reasoning strategy RLVR incentivizes, and whether the learned strategy generalizes from in-distribution training to OOD scenarios or quietly collapses. We therefore propose a research framework that surfaces the model’s reasoning process and admits a controlled distribution shift between training and evaluation. The principles are: (1) Clean OOD Generalization. We adopt synthetic tasks following prior controlled LLM studies ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Chu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2025a ) , enabling a clean separation between the training and testing distributions for studying OOD generalization. (2) Explicit Reasoning Strategies. To diagnose reasoning strategies, the tasks must surface a small set of clearly identifiable strategies. The open-ended flexibility of real-world math or coding tasks works against this need for clean strategy categorization. (3) Reasoning Strategy Diversity. While the strategies must be categorizable, the framework must also allow multiple candidate strategies, so that generalization can be studied by observing which one RLVR selects. From this aspect, the homogeneous function-simulation tasks in Yuan et al. (2026) fall short, as they only exercise the “composing” reasoning strategy and calculation of function outputs. The Inversion Task. We instantiate these principles via an inversion task on synthetic string functions, which reverses the direction of Yuan et al. (2026) : given the source code of a function f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) f(\cdot) and a target output y y , the LLM is asked to recover one or more digit-string inputs x x satisfying f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y . This mirrors two real-world reasoning settings: solving math equations, where one reasons backward from a constraint to its solutions, and tracing program bugs, where one infers an upstream cause from an observed output. Crucially, the inversion task admits several reward-compatible strategies: analytical derivation, case analysis, and brute-force enumeration. It thus satisfies principles (2) and (3), while the next subsection addresses principle (1). 3.2 Task Design We turn the inversion task above into a concrete training-and-evaluation suite, including (i) a library of functions with a function-level train/held-out split, (ii) OOD tests that probe the learned strategy for easy-to-hard generalization, and (iii) evaluation metrics. Function Design for Held-out Training/Evaluation. We construct the training and testing sets to use distinct functions f f , preventing the LLM from memorizing function-specific patterns. We therefore compose 24 non-bijective functions (many-to-one, so one output y y has multiple valid inputs x x ) (full list in Sec. A.2 ) and provide their definitions and Python code inside the prompt of every inversion task. Following Yuan et al. (2026) , we split these functions into training and evaluation sets: 18 functions are used for RL training, and 6 strictly disjoint functions are held out for evaluation. This held-out slice forms the easiest test of generalization: same prompt interface, same input/output regime, only the underlying function is unseen. It serves as the in-distribution check that RLVR has learned to perform inversion. From this baseline, we then move to the easy-to-hard OOD generalization tests below, which are our main probe of reasoning-strategy generalization. The training set contains 50k tasks, and each evaluation set contains 1,024 tasks. Easy-to-hard OOD Generalization. As Fig. 1 a , we design the in-domain and OOD tasks to differ along controlled axes. For the inversion task f ⁡ ( x ) = y f(x)=y , the in-domain scenarios train and evaluate the LLM on outputs y y of length 4–6 and require 2 candidate solutions per prompt. From this baseline, we design four easy-to-hard OOD axes: (1) More Answers raises the number of requested solutions to a random integer between 3 and 6, demanding more computation and reliability to produce enough valid solutions. (2) Longer Outputs increases the target output to length 6–10, lengthening the digit chain that must be inverted. (3) Longer Outputs & More Answers combines the two axes above. (4) Length Change represents the largest shift: our in-distribution function family is designed so that y y and x x share the same length, but the Length-Change functions differ in the lengths of y y and x x (full list in Sec. A.2 ). Each OOD evaluation set contains 1,024 randomly generated tasks as above. Accuracy Scoring. We compute accuracy based on whether the predicted solutions are correct with an outcome-based verifier. Each solution is scored semantically by executing the reference function and checking whether its output matches y y . Let k k be the effective answer requirement and m m be the number of submitted solutions; accuracy is acc = min ⁡ ( correct_unique , k ) / max ⁡ ( k , m ) \mathrm{acc}=\min(\text{correct\_unique},k)/\max(k,m) . This rewards answers that are both distinct and correct, and penalizes over-generation reward hacking. 3.3 Training We train Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) and adopt the improvements from DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , especially the filtering of groups with zero reward variance. This filtering is crucial both in the early stage of training, when the LLM is still developing its strategy with low accuracy, and in the late stage, when in-distribution accuracy has been high. We select this base model because our synthetic task lies on the boundary of its capabilities, requiring RL to incentivize correct reasoning strategies. Design details are in Sec. A.3 . By closely observing it on the in-distribution and the four easy-to-hard OOD sets, as in Fig. 2 , we observe the nuanced OOD reasoning strategy collapse. Reasoning Strategy Categorization. Our synthetic tasks are specially constructed to understand the RLVR reasoning strategy generalization in a controllable way, as explained in Sec. 3.1 . As in Fig. 3 , we can clearly attribute two primary strategies: derivation , which structurally reverses f f and only conduct case-analysis when needed, and enumeration , which directly guess all the digits all at once, being much less efficient. To make this binary classification revealing the traits of reasoning strategies, we treat purely brute-force enumeration as “enumeration,” and everything else as “derivation.” In practice, we employ an LLM judge empowered by Gemini-3.0-Flash to classify the reasoning traces (clarification of our setup, details, and verification of LLM judge in Sec. B.1 ). From ID to OOD Collapse. Fig. 2(a) tracks accuracy during RL on the ID set and the four OOD sets, and Fig. 2(b) shows which strategies produce these responses. On in-distribution tasks, the Mono model learns the effective strategy of derivation in most cases and achieves high accuracy (as Fig. 2 , ID columns). However, its failure in OOD scenarios, e.g. , the novel functions of lenchange, is not solely due to longer reasoning or more computation. Rather, its reasoning skill of derivation acquired disappears on OOD tasks and gives way to the inefficient brute-force enumeration, which proposes all the digits of x x simultaneously, without utilizing the structure of the function f f . The majority of failures are caused by loops that enumerate all possible digits until reaching the token limits. Here, collapse refers to the reasoning strategy: Mono ’s derivation share drops from 85% on ID to below 50% on the three harder OOD sets. Accuracy, in contrast, degrades progressively as the shift grows: it stays above 80% on More Answers, the mildest shift, and drops to 6% on Length Change. Such an observation is surprising as it challenges RLVR generalization: the reasoning strategy already incentivized in RL fails to generalize despite identical task formats . As mentioned in Sec. 1 and Sec. 3 , this observation focuses on the meta-level reasoning skills of LLMs and is subtle and distinct from prior work. First, it is not a base-model limitation: the same model reaches ≈ 90 % \approx{}90\% on in-distribution non-bijective inversion. Second, it is not reward hacking : the LLM uses the correct and efficient derivation strategy for in-distribution evaluation rather than spurious shortcuts. We refer to this phenomenon as reasoning-strategy collapse , which motivates our central question: which training signal enables RLVR to generalize a reasoning pattern to OOD scenarios? Takeaway 1 Reasoning Strategy Collapse: Even though RLVR has incentivized the correct reasoning strategies for in-distribution tasks, the LLM might drastically change to ineffective strategies on OOD tasks despite identical task formats, undermining the generalization of RLVR. 4.2 Mixed Model: Enhancing OOD Generalization via Bijective Inversion The derivation reasoning strategy, avoiding pure enumeration, is thus our key to understanding RLVR generalization. Our intervention, therefore, is not to propose training tasks that are closer to the evaluation or simply harder than the existing training tasks, but a set of new tasks that more directly incentivize the derivation strategy. In fact, this is also why RLVR could bring improvements to multiple reasoning domains for LLMs in previous works ( Liu et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . Specifically, we propose using bijective functions as f f (both injective and surjective) to eliminate uncertainty in non-bijective tasks and encourage derivation via larger certainty. Enhancing OOD Generalization. Concretely, we co-train on bijective inversion with a 1 : 1 1{:}1 with the original non-bijective tasks, so this model is called Mixed . As shown in Fig. 2(b) , this almost doubles the utilization of derivation strategy compared with the Mono model, and leads to significantly better OOD evaluation (Fig. 2(a) ), especially on the novel functions of LenChange. Therefore, the incorporation of bijective inversion effectively improves the RLVR reasoning generalization. We have controlled the data recipe and training configuration for a fair comparison between the two models (details Sec. A.3 ) and additionally verified the main conclusions with multiple runs in Sec. B.2.4 . Why Unexpected? This is a surprising observation because it contradicts three natural intuitions: (1) bijective tasks ask for a single answer, so they are further from the multi-answer evaluation; (2) they are not clearly harder by the training reward or by intrinsic difficulty (details in Sec. B.2 ); and (3) they do not change the in-distribution accuracy notably (Fig. 2 ). These further suggest that the meta-level reasoning strategies are the essential element for RLVR generalization. For scientific rigor, we have conducted additional experiments in Sec. B.2 to eliminate the confounding factors other than reasoning strategies. Specifically, our controllable experiments show that the improvement is not primarily explained by: (1) a special set of evaluation; (2) increasing the diversity of training tasks; and (3) increasing the difficulty of training tasks. Such analysis further motivates us to understand how the reasoning strategies that generalize better are incentivized. Takeaway 2 Incorporating tasks that are even further from the OOD evaluation, i.e. , bijective inversion, enhances generalization via encouraging the more effective reasoning strategy. 5 Bits Per Token Shapes Reasoning Strategies and Generalization With Sec. 4 revealing reasoning strategies as the central driver of RLVR generalization, this section answers two questions: (1) what makes a reasoning strategy effective, e.g. , derivation over enumeration, which we frame as bits of information generated per token (Sec. 5.1 ); and (2) how an outcome-only RLVR reward implicitly supervises the reasoning process and selects effective strategies (Sec. 5.2 ). However, this experiment hints at potential future work: the principle of reasoning strategies and bits per token, though discussed primarily for reasoning tasks in this paper, may also improve RLVR in agentic settings. 7 Conclusion This paper investigates reasoning strategies as a crucial factor for RLVR generalization. On a controllable framework of non-bijective string equations with clearly defined OOD generalization, RLVR teaches the derivation strategy in-distribution, yet the model falls back to ineffective enumeration on OOD tasks. Co-training with bijective tasks restores derivation and enhances OOD generalization, which motivates our theory: effective reasoning strategies contribute more bits per token and are implicitly rewarded by RLVR. Our broader analyses further support the role of reasoning strategies in LLM generalization, and we discuss limitations in Sec. H . We hope our study can inspire RL recipes that improve generalization by controlling reasoning strategies. A.3 Training Details Implementation. We run RL experiments with VERL/HybridFlow ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) , using the GRPO objective ( Shao et al., 2024 ) with the DAPO-style filtering of zero-reward-variance groups ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . The policy is initialized from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; rollouts are generated with vllm , and actor/reference models are sharded with FSDP. Training is conducted on one node with 8 NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs, approximately 1 day. Reward. We follow common RLVR practice and construct the reward by 0.1 of format reward, including the thinking format and number of solutions, and 0.9 of the accuracy scoring. Core hyperparameters. Unless otherwise stated, we train for 200 update steps with a prompt batch size of 16, one PPO epoch per update, actor learning rate 10 − 6 10^{-6} , clip ratio 0.2 0.2 , entropy coefficient 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and gradient clipping at 1.0 1.0 . We use GRPO groups of 16 sampled rollouts per prompt, with sampling temperature 1.0 1.0 , top- p p of 1.0 1.0 , and no top- k k truncation. The maximum prompt length is 1,024 tokens and the maximum response length is 8,192 tokens; the short-budget intervention in Sec. 5.3 changes only this response budget to 5 ​ k 5\mathrm{k} tokens. We do not use a learned reward model or KL penalty in these controlled experiments; rewards are computed by the verifier in Sec. A.1 . Validation is run every 20 steps with greedy decoding ( temperature =0, one rollout per prompt). A.4 Selection of Base Model This section explains why we decided to use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as our base model. For controlled studies of LLM post-training, the base model is part of the experimental design: if it is too weak, failures mostly measure missing task competence; if it is too strong, the task saturates before RL exposes what the reward is selecting. This is the same methodological motivation behind prior controlled reasoning studies ( Ye et al., 2025a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , which choose settings where the target behavior is observable, the verifier is clean, and the training dynamics remain diagnostic. Since our goal is to reveal a nuanced RLVR generalization failure rather than to maximize absolute accuracy, the appropriate base model is one that can solve the in-distribution task after RL but still leaves enough room for the learned reasoning strategy to vary and collapse OOD. Additional Base Models. We tried Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) and Qwen3-4B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2025 ) under the same inversion task setup. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct does not provide a suitable initialization for our question: after RL on non-bijective tasks, it reaches only 27.1 % 27.1\% on in-distribution non-bijective inversion. This performance indicates that the model falls into the category of less capable base model, has not yet acquired reliable inversion reasoning or the basic execution skills needed for our analysis. Failures in this regime would mostly reflect insufficient task competence, rather than a strategy-level OOD generalization gap. So we exclude Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as our base model. Qwen3-4B-Instruct has the opposite issue: it is already too strong for this controlled study. Its in-distribution non-bijective inversion accuracy reaches 97.8 % 97.8\% after just 20 steps of RL training, indicating that our controlled study has not significantly influenced the model’s behavior yet. This leaves little room for RL to reveal a meaningful strategy-acquisition process, because the model is close to saturation before the training dynamics become informative. Conclusion. Using controlled study to investigate LLM is a co-design across the model, task, data. For our purpose, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is the appropriate operating point because it makes the central comparison identifiable: after RL, both Mono and Mixed solve the in-distribution non-bijective inversion task at about 91 91 – 92 % 92\% , so the source-task competence, prompt understanding, and verifier-compatible answer behavior are already established. The remaining failure is therefore not that the model cannot solve the task, but that the reasoning strategy learned on the source distribution does not necessarily transfer OOD. This is exactly the phenomenon our paper aims to reveal. If we used a weaker model, the same OOD failures would be confounded with missing basic skills; if we used a saturated model, RL would provide too little behavioral change to analyze strategy selection. Making the task much longer or harder would similarly mix our target failure with arithmetic, context-length, and execution errors. Thus, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is a principled choice for exposing reasoning-strategy collapse under already favorable conditions for RLVR generalization.
